title: Hubble’s 13-Billion-Year-Old Firework Show!
summary: What’s red, white, and blue and 13 billion years old? A star cluster that looks like a giant sparkler in space! NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope just released a stunning new picture of NGC 6426, a globular cluster—a huge, round group of stars held together by gravity. This cluster is ancient. It formed when the universe was just a baby, only about 700 million years after the Big Bang. That makes it one of the oldest things in our galaxy! The stars in the picture aren’t really red, white, and blue like a flag. The colors come from special filters on Hubble that show different types of light. Blue stars are hotter, and red stars are cooler. Scientists love studying clusters like this because they’re like time capsules. The stars have very few heavy elements—mostly just hydrogen and helium, like the early universe. The cluster even has two groups of stars that formed at different times. The second group was born after the first big stars exploded, spreading new elements around. Those explosions helped create the stuff that makes up planets—and you! Hubble took this picture as part of a project to learn how our Milky Way galaxy grew up. So next time you see fireworks, think of this cosmic sparkler that’s been shining for 13 billion years.
why_it_matters: Studying ancient stars helps us learn where we come from, because the elements that make up our bodies were created in big star explosions long ago.

background_read: The Hubble Space Telescope is a powerful camera floating in space that has taken pictures of the universe for over 30 years. Globular clusters are some of the oldest objects in our galaxy, containing hundreds of thousands of stars packed tightly together.
NGC 6426 is one such cluster, and its ancient stars give clues about what the early universe was like only 700 million years after the Big Bang.
The Milky Way (our home galaxy, with over 100 billion stars) grew by collecting clusters like this one, making them time capsules of galaxy history.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope and scientists studying the Milky Way.

WHAT: Hubble took a new picture of globular cluster NGC 6426, which is 13 billion years old, has stars mostly of hydrogen and helium, and contains two populations of stars that formed at different times.
WHERE: The cluster sits in the Milky Way galaxy, far away in space.
WHY: To understand how our galaxy formed and what the early universe was made of by studying these ancient 'time capsules.'

perspectives.description: The picture shows that the universe has been making stars for billions of years, and we get to see this beautiful cosmic sparkler.
Some people think expensive telescopes like Hubble cost a lot of money that could be spent on helping people on Earth instead.
For scientists, clusters like NGC 6426 are like history books, telling the story of how our galaxy and everything in it came to be.
